extracted.intended_audience: Applicants to the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship Program (undergraduate seniors and early graduate students preparing GRFP applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for preparing NSF GRFP application materials, especially the personal statement and research statement, emphasizing alignment with the solicitation and demonstrating readiness for graduate research. Includes suggestions on project scope, structure, background, and addressing intellectual merit and broader impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the NSF solicitation closely
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully read the entire solicitation for the NSF GRFP for the year you apply; keep key phrases and directions from the solicitation in your drafts to make sure you are on track.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes reading the current solicitation and using its language in your personal and research statements to ensure alignment with current requirements and priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal statement — identify and tell a coherent career story
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing the personal statement, identify the 'story' you want to tell about your career: explain how past experiences moved you toward graduate school and beyond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer the question of how all of your past experiences lead to your future goals; this narrative thread should be present across sections of the statement to present a cohesive arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research project scope appropriate for 5–6 years
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose a project that is appropriate for a 5–6 year timeframe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the research scope so it is realistic for the duration of graduate training (not too large or too small) and aligns with expected PhD/project timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research project structured with distinct milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the proposed project so it has distinct milestones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the project into clear stages or milestones that show planfulness and feasibility over the doctoral period; reviewers look for a structured plan rather than vague long-term goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project suited to your background; provide a convincing background section
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose a project that is suited to your background. If suitability is not obvious, write a thorough and convincing background section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly connect your prior experiences and skills to the proposed work. The author insists on a strong background section regardless — it helps establish preparedness and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate intellectual merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the proposed project compelling in intellectual merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the scientific or scholarly importance: novelty, advancement of knowledge, rigor of ideas and approach. Tie the work to substantive research questions rather than only broader outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate broader impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the proposed project compelling in broader impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how the work benefits society, education, diversity, outreach, or other impacts outside the immediate research contribution; be concrete about activities or outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how the work fills a knowledge gap
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state how the proposed research is filling a knowledge gap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the existing gap in the literature or practice and show how your project addresses it; this supports both intellectual merit and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe applications and future directions
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss potential applications and future directions that could come from the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay out plausible next steps, applied uses, or lines of inquiry that extend from your proposed research to demonstrate broader relevance and long-term thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify who can be involved besides yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate who else can be involved in the work besides yourself (collaborators, mentors, other participants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming potential collaborators, advisors, or communities that would engage with the project strengthens feasibility and broader impact planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete past research experiences as evidence of readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw on prior research experiences (e.g., REU) to support claims about preparedness and to provide material for the research statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author used their REU heavily when writing the research statement; concrete examples of hands-on research demonstrate capability and inform the proposed project's plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance showing the person and proposing a solid project
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that NSF 'funds the person, not the project' — show your potential as a researcher while still proposing an appropriate, well-scoped project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate intellectual promise, trajectory, and personal qualities (e.g., independence, creativity) alongside a feasible research plan; both dimensions matter to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult past successful applications and recommended timelines/resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use external resources such as databases of past winners, annotated successful applications, and suggested timelines to inform preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recommends Alex Lang, Mallory Ladd (timeline and examples), and Claire McKay Bowen (annotated winning excerpts) as helpful resources — review examples and timelines but ensure you follow the current solicitation.
